definition: The highest and lowest price an asset reached over the past year. Traders watch these levels because prices often react around them — but they are reference points, not guarantees.
How many assets rose vs fell in a session. A healthy rally has many advancers; if few stocks rise while an index climbs, the move is narrow and fragile.
The average daily price range over ~14 days. Bigger ATR = bigger typical daily swings = more volatility.
A moving average with upper and lower bands set ~2 standard deviations away. Prices touching the bands are statistically stretched — context, not a signal to act.
How widely market moves are shared. 'Broad' means most assets move together; 'narrow' means a few big names carry the index.
A licensed firm that executes buy/sell orders for investors. MarketPulse teaches you how to read markets — any investing happens through regulated brokers, never through us.
Bull = sustained rising prices and optimism; bear = sustained falling prices and caution. From the animals' attack motions: horns thrust up, paws strike down.
A chart bar showing open, high, low and close for a period. The 'body' spans open→close; 'wicks' show the extremes. Green/emerald usually means close > open.
India's daily price movement bands (e.g. ±10-20% for many stocks) designed to slow panic moves. When hit, trading pauses or bounds apply.
How two things move together, from -1 (opposite) to +1 (together). MarketPulse correlates DXY, crude, gold, VIX and 10Y moves against each index to map cross-asset pressure.
MarketPulse's measure of how macro drivers (dollar index, 10Y yield, crude, gold, VIX) co-move with an index. E.g. a strong dollar often pressures emerging-market indices.
An electronic account that holds shares in dematerialized form — required for investing in India's markets alongside a trading account.
The US dollar's value vs a basket of major currencies. A rising DXY usually means global dollar liquidity tightening — often pressure on emerging markets and commodities.
A company's reported profit. Earnings seasons can reprice stocks quickly when results beat or miss expectations.
An exchange-traded fund — a basket of investments that trades like a single stock, letting people own many assets at once.
The organized marketplace (NSE/BSE in India, NYSE/Nasdaq in the US) where listed securities are bought and sold.
Foreign vs Domestic Institutional Investors. Their daily net buying/selling is tracked as a sentiment gauge for Indian markets.
A company's underlying business reality: revenue, profits, debt, growth. Fundamental analysis asks 'what is this worth?'; technical analysis asks 'what is the trend?'
When price opens noticeably above/below the previous close (often on overnight news). Gaps reveal how news re-priced the asset between sessions.
A position meant to offset risk in another (like insurance for portfolios). MarketPulse maps where institutions may be *forced* to hedge via its volume-pressure proxy.
A fund that simply holds an index's constituents, giving market returns at low cost — often the first instrument beginners study.
Large managed money: mutual funds, pension funds, insurers, hedge funds. Their scale moves markets, which is why volume-based proxies of their behavior matter.
Within a single trading day. Intraday moves can be noisy; MarketPulse focuses on daily structure.
How easily something can be bought/sold without moving its price. High liquidity = many participants and tight spreads.
Moving Average Convergence Divergence: the gap between fast and slow trend averages. A positive histogram means short momentum is above longer trend — a momentum read, not advice.
The share of assets above their 50-day averages, advancers vs decliners, and similar measures — 'how many boats are rising?'.
The overall mood of participants. MarketPulse measures it from news tone plus price/volume structure, always shown with its evidence.
The tendency of recent direction to persist short-term. MarketPulse weighs recent returns and RSI in its momentum factor.
The average price of the last N days, redrawn daily. Price above its 50-day average is a simple trend marker; below it, the opposite.
A running total that adds volume on up-days and subtracts it on down-days. Its slope shows whether volume flows with or against the price trend.
Open, High, Low, Close — the four prices that summarize each day's trading.
Price divided by annual earnings per share. Roughly, how many years of current profits the price represents. Compare within sectors, not across all stocks.
Everything a person owns across investments, viewed as a whole. Managing risk across a portfolio matters more than any single pick.
0-100 score of recent up vs down days (Wilder, 1978). ≥70 often read as overbought; ≤30 oversold. A momentum gauge — never a buy/sell signal.
Actual volatility measured from recent returns (MarketPulse uses 20 days, annualized). Contrast with 'implied' volatility from option prices.
A price zone where selling has repeatedly stopped advances. Descriptive of the past, not a promise about the future.
Simple Moving Average — see Moving Average (SMA).
Zones where buying/selling have historically stepped in. Useful context for where attention gathers — not a guarantee prices will respect them.
How spread out numbers are around their average. MarketPulse uses it in VWAP z-scores: how unusual is today's price vs its recent volume-weighted average?
A price zone where buying has repeatedly stopped declines. Past behavior, not a future guarantee.
Reading price/volume patterns to understand trend and participation. MarketPulse uses standard indicators deterministically — the AI never invents them.
Shares/contracts traded in a period. Confirms or questions a move: big move + big volume = broad participation.
MarketPulse's honest label for estimating institutional accumulation/distribution from public data: up/down volume ratio, OBV slope, volume z-score. A proxy — real order-flow is private.
The CBOE Volatility Index — the market's expectation of near-term US equity volatility, derived from option prices. Rising VIX = rising caution.
MarketPulse's filter for *how fast* fear is changing: 5-day VIX change measured against its own history. Fast spikes shift reads toward 'Uncertain'.
Volume-Weighted Average Price — the average price weighted by how much traded there. Institutions benchmark execution against it.
How statistically stretched price is vs its rolling VWAP, in standard deviations. |z| > 2 = extended move. Deterministic filter feeding the AI — never advice.
The annual return of a bond, e.g. the US 10-year yield — the closest thing to a global 'risk-free' benchmark that everything else prices against.
Where price sits between its 52-week low (0%) and high (100%). MarketPulse shows it so beginners see range context at a glance.
